snippet: Self-Improving AI Agents: From Karpathy's Lab t - TeamDay.ai # Self-Improving AI Agents: From Karpathy's Lab to a Live Hedge Fund # Self-Improving AI Agents: From Karpathy's Lab to a Live Hedge Fund In early March 2026, Andrej Karpathy released autoresearch— a framework where AI agents autonomously run ML experiments overnight, keep what works, revert what doesn't. Within days, the repo had 28,000 stars. Shopify's CEO ran it and got a 0.8B parameter model that outperformed his previous 1.6B model. Karpathy called the experience of watching agents catch optimization oversights he'd missed over two decades "wild." Then Chris Worsey, founder of General Intelligence Capital, did something nobody expected. He took the same loop and pointed it at financial markets. ## The Autoresearch Loop Karpathy's insight is deceptively simple. The core loop: 1. Agent reads the code (train.py) and forms a hypothesis 2. Agent modifies the code 3. System runs a 5-minute training experiment 4. System evaluates the result (validation bits-per-byte) 5. If improved: git commit. If worse: git reset 6. Repeat That's it. No human in the loop. No review process. Just: try something, measure the outcome, keep or revert. At ~12 experiments per hour, the system runs 100+ experiments overnight. In one documented session, 126 experiments produced 23 improvements — an 18% keep rate. The validation metric dropped steadily from 0.9979 to 0.9697 while the human slept. From Code to Capital Chris Worsey saw the pattern and asked: what if the thing being optimized isn't code — but prompts? And what if the loss function isn't validation loss — but Sharpe ratio? He built ATLAS — 25 AI agents organized into four layers, each with a specific role in the investment process. ## The Darwinian Loop Here's where search meets natural selection 1. Score every agent by rolling Sharpe ratio 2. Identify the worst performer 3. Rewrite its prompt — one targeted modification 4. Test for 5 trading days 5. Evaluate: did the Sharpe improve? 6. Keep (git commit) or revert (git reset) Daily, the system adjusts weights. Top quartile agents get a 1.05x multiplier. Bottom quartile gets 0.95x. Weights range from 0.3 (nearly silenced) to 2.5 (highly trusted). The CIO layer uses these weights to determine how much each agent's opinion matters. Over 378 trading days: 54 prompt modifications attempted. 16 survived. 37 reverted. A 30% keep rate — remarkably close to Karpathy's 18% on code modifications. ## Specific Agent Improvements The Financials agent went from catastrophically bad to positive. Not by a human rewriting its prompt based on intuition — by the system testing modifications against real market outcomes and keeping what worked. ## The Principle Generalizes Agents + Measurable Outcomes + Keep/Revert Loop = Self-Improvement 1. Specialized agents with distinct roles (not one agent trying to do everything) 2. A measurable fitness function (Sharpe ratio, validation loss, or... ranking improvements, conversion rates, engagement metrics) 3. A loop that tests modifications and keeps what works 4. Time for the evolutionary pressure to compound fatigue curves. Karpathy releases a loop for evolving code. Within a week, someone applies it to financial markets and deploys it with real capital. The framework is open source. The infrastructure costs $20/month. The results beat most human fund managers. The question isn't whether AI agents can improve themselves. They already are. The question is: what else can this loop optimize? The keep rate is 30%. The other 70% get reverted. That's not failure — that's how evolution works. Most mutations don't help. The ones that do compound. Prompts are the new weights. Outcomes are the new loss function. And the agents are getting better while we sleep.
